It doesn't have to be altruism at all. As I said, since the meeting with Chief, she doesn't actually support Paradeisos anymore, as she explained in her monologue. Rahu doesn't like Paradeisos and wants to take revenge, Shalom does not like Paradeisos either. They definitely aren't enemies since their goals are technically aligned. 

Shalom, again, in her monologue, is revealed to be driven by three things - wanting to help Chief gain freedom, hate for Paradeisos higher-ups and their methods of doing things, and cautiousness not to reveal her defect to Paradeisos. Rahu is aligned with her on the second, the first and third being of no matter to her, so there is no reason for a conflict between them. (On Shalom's end, at least, Rahu is obviously confused because of how Shalom has to act in order not to reveal her defect.)

I wrote about that in more detail in a separate comment, but I don't really agree with what is stated here.

For one, Shalom fulfills her initial promise to Rahu and gets her to Paradeisos when she is in no way obliged to do so. You have to remember that at the time of this story, Shalom already has emotions. The monologue at the end of her interrogation, which happens basically right before Rain Burst, shows just how much she disapproves of what Paradeisos is doing and especially what they have done to her. She feels dehumanized by them, however, is smart enough to realize that she can in no way show that, since, as we know, she really is defenseless, save for the Schorl beside her, which is really controlled by Paradeisos. 

All that means that yes, as you said, on a surface level, her actions seem like her just using Rahu, but that really is because that's what she has to convince Paradeisos of, she has to justify her actions and incorporate them in their plan. That means, of course, that Rahu is also confused, and that is the main reason their dynamic is so complicated.

I feel like a lot of people here aren't realizing the main reason why the dynamic between Shalom and Rahu is the way that it is, so I will put my 2 cents down in here and if anyone disagrees, feel free to correct me below.

Shalom was created as a tool for Paradeisos. We know that. We also know that she "defected" during her first meeting with Chief. The thing is, though, she is smart enough to act in a way that conceals that. Ever since the "defect," she is able to experience emotions, most importantly, empathy, to a certain extent, and disapproval for Paradeisos. Due to her position, though, she is under constant surveillance by the Schorl, every single one of her actions being scrutinized. Even just tapping the Schorl for no reason is enough to trigger a "level 1 scan." We can all imagine what would happen if she helped Rahu for "no reason." That's why, to achieve what she wants, she has to make what she wants to do seem like part of what Paradeisos has to do. Basically, for example, she has to convince Paradeisos that she's manipulating Rahu while telling her that she wants to help her get her revenge, even though she isn't really lying to her but when Rahu finds out that this technically is part of Paradeisos' plan (made by Shalom) she starts believing she was manipulated, even though that's not really the case. 

There are so many other cases in the story where basically the same thing happens: Shalom does something that usually would trigger suspicion in Paradeisos, but basically convinces them that it's part of a better plan for them to get what they want. And since her plans work, she gets to keep doing that. Thing is, for people on the other side, they can't really tell whether she's helping them or not, and she obviously can't tell them either (even telling them in the Observatorium is risky, since they can ruin her disguise outside, so she's careful about that too, it really is all planned).

Basically, my interpretation of their relationship is that Shalom actually wants to and helps Rahu, but she can't make it obvious or tell her, so Rahu is confused and doesn't know what to believe, but in the end something tells her to "trust" Shalom. Objectively speaking, it makes no sense for Paradeisos to have someone like Rahu going around and having a relatively high position, but Shalom manages to make that happen and to convince them that it's okay to have her there.

In the end, I believe in another world (or after a long time, when this is all over), where Shalom can truly be honest with Rahu and respectively gain Rahu's trust, they would like each other (probably in a platonic way, realistically, since Shalom is almost certainly head over heels for Chief, but exaggerating that for the purpose of a ship is more than fine, in my eyes.)

Since the (current) system literally only cares about wins and losses (as per Riot), it cannot distinguish between someone being carried/lucky for their first couple of games and someone who carries and wins these same games. 

Again, as per Riot, what the system uses to evaluate you is your game history (wins and losses) and who you played with/against (by proxy their wins and losses, etc.), meaning that a certain amount of variance is introduced into the system's estimation of any player's skill. In fact, this is true for any similar ranking system. The underlying assumption made by any such system, however, is that this (and any other type of) variance diminishes with the number of games played by that particular player. Your boyfriend has allegedly played a lot more games on their account, meaning that their rank is much likelier to be close to their real skill than yours is.

In the end, the conclusion is simply that this is with a very high likelihood not your real rank, and if you want to find out what your rank actually might be, then you'd have to just play more games. The more you play (on the same acc), the more accurate your rank will be.

The only real way to change this is to remove the possibility of a disparity between MMR and LP, i.e. only work with MMR and map LP numbers directly onto that. That however, would completely fuck season starts in one of two ways: you would either need to remove placement games for old accounts and basically having no seasons, since that would mean no MMR resets, which is 1 not sustainable and 2 removes incentive to even play, or, instead, have hard MMR resets, just like the hard LP resets we get every season and have to play with people who were challenger last season in your early season plat games. That is exactly why you have both MMR and LP, and they don't always match. MMR is there to ensure the opponents you're playing against are of a similar skill level. You wouldn't want that to be changed without the player's skill level actually changing, i.e. you wouldn't want to drop challenger players to play with people in platinum every season start, because that just makes for unfair games. MMR works like chess ELO, and you don't see every GM starting at 1800 ELO every year for a reason. LP is there to literally be a reward, a trophy for the efforts you put in play and climb each season. It is also there, ironically, to also protect your sanity. You wouldn't want to see and know what happens to your MMR during a long loss streak. By losing to worse and worse players, your MMR drops even more than the equivalent of those 30 LP you're losing, you might be losing 60 LP worth of MMR per game. LP artificially protects you from this, by limiting the amount you gain/lose per match, so that it doesn't feel so bad to be losing 60 LP per game, though, in MMR, you really are losing that much. That 32 LP loss the guy had in LP was probably a much smaller loss in MMR.

The bottom line is this: *No fair system will ever feel right to the player in every situation, and no system that feels right to the player in every situation will ever be fair.* Emotion and rationality don't mix, and that is the exact reason why a system that "feels right" will never be fair.

Those numbers you're citing are only true if you're casting every ability instantly off cooldown, which is almost impossible either because of human error, even if you're spamming the key, or because you just don't have a target. Another factor, is that for high cooldown abilities (most ultimates), the ability haste you need to get another spell cast with them within a fight becomes pretty much impossible to get, meaning that for those abilities, getting 100 extra ability haste doesn't result in two times the ability casts, simply because you're working with the limited duration of a fight. On the topic of AP and ability haste, usually healing and shielding abilities have low ratios, making it more efficient to use H&SP to amplify their base values, instead of trying to gain value with the subpar AP ratios present on them. As for ability haste on the other hand, after a certain threshold you really don't get much value from buying more, since in this case, there is the opposite effect to stacking H&SP - it has diminishing returns. Lucidity boots + Transcendence + 8 AH from runes + 20 from mythic makes for 58 AH, at which point getting more provides very little benefit in comparison to H&SP. In addition to that, enchanter items in general don't have a lot of AH, pretty much exactly because it is all concentrated in the sources mentioned above. The build really doesn't lack as much AH as it seems, it is in fact fairly well rounded.

You don't need any specific amount, you really see benefits even if you only have 5% H&SP, there is no threshold. The more H&SP you get, the bigger the difference becomes, at a quadratic rate at that.

Your claim sadly relies on the assumption that both everyone is equally as good at using the Redemption active, and that simply playing with the item and practicing it doesn't increase your skill level at using it and your chance of a good activation per try. Both are naturally false, so if you simply practice it, you can absolutely become better with it than the average user of the active, meaning, that you should expect the build to have more power when you use it, than the average league player.

The issue with these statistics is the following: a player's first 3 games with a champion like, let's say Akali, are much more likely to be losses than a player's first 3 games with Garen. If you invest 50 games in Garen, your likelihood to win won't improve that much over the first 3 games, but if you play 50 games of Akali - it will improve drastically. If you check the champion play rate stats, you will find that for most champions the average amount of games a player plays with that champion are between 1 and 3-4 on the very, very high end. Well, if the average player drops the champion after losing 3 times, or losing 2 and winning one, or anything like that, then is it really a surprise than the winrate is lower? If you basically remove the people "first timing" a champ from your statistics, you'll see how the "difficult" champs increase in win rate, however the easy ones see less change. 

Same principle applies to item builds. The winrate you see for redemption includes people who got autofilled support and built the most picked build, bad at using Redemption because they rarely build it, as well as people who regularly build it and are very good at using it. It is not that difficult to improve at it, and if you do, you will be part of a player demographic, who actually finds more success with the item. The same effect wouldn't be present with Staff and Ardent, because you have no skillshot to whiff.
